Value averaging or plain dollar-cost averaging: the rule that buys more after a crash, and the cash it has to keep waiting

Value averaging tops a fund up to a target path each month, so it asks for much more money after prices fall and less, or even a sale, after they rise. See what that does to the same monthly savings through a crash, why a lower purchase price is not guaranteed, what the waiting cash earned in treasury bills since 2006 and how the account changes the tax.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Both investors save $500 a month from pay and start with $3,000 in cash. Dollar-cost averaging invests each $500 as it arrives and leaves the starting cash alone. Value averaging puts each saving into a cash pot and buys whatever it takes to keep the fund on a path growing 5% a year plus the new savings, selling units when the fund is ahead of the path. The fund earns 5% in ordinary years and falls 25% in year 2; the next year makes up exactly two ordinary years. Cash earns 2.5%. Every number is a hypothetical calculation before tax, not a forecast of any fund. A lower average purchase price does not by itself mean more money at the end: the money that waits in cash matters too. In the crash path the cash pot ran out in 1 month; the largest purchase it could not pay in a single month was $79, and the fund stayed behind its target until prices recovered.

The central idea

Dollar-cost averaging invests the same amount from every paycheque. Value averaging invests whatever it takes to keep the fund on a target path, so after a fall it asks for more money exactly when prices are low. That sounds like a better version of the same idea, but the extra money has to wait somewhere in cash beforehand, the rebound itself does much of the catching up, and the rule may ask for more than you have. With the same savings, the two can end within a few hundred dollars of each other, in either order. Value averaging is a way to plan for crash-time buying, not a way to remove market risk.

01

Two rules for the same paycheque

Suppose you set aside CAD 500 from each month’s pay for a balanced fund. The simplest rule is to invest the CAD 500 every month, whatever the market is doing. That is dollar-cost averaging: a fixed amount buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high.

Value averaging is a more demanding rule. Instead of fixing the amount you invest, you fix the value you want the fund to have each month, and invest whatever closes the gap. If the fund has fallen, the gap is large and you invest more than CAD 500. If it has risen faster than planned, the gap is small, and under the strict version of the rule you sell units. People who worry about a crash are often drawn to it because it turns a fall into a planned buying opportunity. This guide asks what it actually does to the same savings, where the extra money comes from, and what the waiting money earns.

02

How the target path works

The calculator uses the most common form of the target. Each month the target grows by a chosen rate and then rises by the month’s saving. With CAD 500 a month and a 5% yearly growth in the target, the target is CAD 500 after the first purchase, about CAD 6,136 after a year, about CAD 12,579 after two years and about CAD 77,182 after ten. That path is simply what the fund would be worth if your monthly savings earned exactly 5% a year.

Each month value averaging compares the fund’s value with the target. Both investors here save the same CAD 500 and start with the same CAD 3,000 already saved. Dollar-cost averaging invests the CAD 500 and leaves the CAD 3,000 in cash. Value averaging puts the CAD 500 into a cash pot beside the fund and pays for each month’s purchase from that pot. Money from any sale goes back into the pot. When the pot is empty, value averaging buys what it can and falls behind its target; the calculator counts those months instead of assuming you can find more money.

One consequence follows straight away. If the fund earns exactly the target rate every year, both rules invest exactly CAD 500 a month and end at the same value, CAD 81,336 after ten years with the defaults. The rules differ only when returns differ from the target, which is to say almost always.

03

What a crash does to each rule

In the default scenario the fund earns 5% in ordinary years, falls 25% through year 2 and recovers in year 3, so that years 2 and 3 together grow exactly as two ordinary years would. The second chart shows what each rule asks you to invest:

  • During the fall, value averaging asks for more each month as the fund slides further below the target, up to about CAD 834 in month 24, the bottom. Over year 2 it invests about CAD 8,849 against CAD 6,000 for dollar-cost averaging, at an average price of about CAD 9.10 a unit.
  • The pot nearly runs dry. By the end of year 2 only about CAD 270 is left, and in month 25 the pot cannot pay the full purchase; it is about CAD 79 short.
  • During the rebound, the fund’s own recovery lifts it back to its target within months, so value averaging invests only about CAD 1,406 in year 3, when prices are still low, and even sells a little near the end of the year. Dollar-cost averaging keeps buying CAD 500 a month through the cheap rebound.
  • The result. After ten years dollar-cost averaging has about CAD 84,686 and value averaging about CAD 84,072, including the cash left in the pot. Value averaging’s average purchase price is about CAD 12.11 a unit against CAD 12.09.

So the rule that buys more at the bottom did not come out ahead. It did buy cheaply in the fall, but it skipped the rebound, and the savings it did not need to invest during the rebound, about CAD 6,576 by year 10, stayed in cash earning 2.5% instead of 5%. Change the crash year and the order can flip. With the crash in year 9 value averaging ends about CAD 176 ahead, but it would have needed up to CAD 2,168 in a single month and its pot was short in 19 months, once by about CAD 15,798, because a fall in a much larger fund needs far more money to fill. The fourth chart puts these totals side by side.

04

The money that waits: what short-term cash has earned since 2006

Value averaging only works if there is cash ready to spend when prices fall. That cash has a cost, and the first chart puts a dated number on it. Statistics Canada publishes the 3-month Government of Canada treasury bill yield each month. Rolling CAD 10,000 over in 3-month bills from September 2006, earning one twelfth of each month’s yield, would have grown to about CAD 13,935 by September 2026. Over the same years the all-items CPI rose from 109.2 to 170.0, about 55.7%, so that balance bought only what about CAD 8,951 bought in 2006. Yields ranged from 0.06% in early 2021 to 5.08% in 2023, and were 2.39% in September 2026.

This is an approximation before tax, not the rate of any savings account. It shows why the size of the pot matters. In the calculator, setting the target growth lower than the fund’s return makes the fund run ahead of its target, so value averaging keeps selling and saving: at 3% the pot grows to about CAD 13,361 and the total falls to about CAD 83,369. Setting it higher keeps the pot empty: at 7% the pot runs out in 12 months and the total is about CAD 84,808, slightly above dollar-cost averaging. A target that is too generous makes the rule demand money you may not have; one that is too modest turns it into a slow way of holding cash, a version of the problem in the guide to waiting for a crash.

05

Accounts and tax: keep the pot inside the same account

The account sets the tax; the fund and the rule do not. A balanced fund held in a TFSA, an RRSP or a taxable account carries the same market risk, but the extra trades value averaging makes are treated differently:

  • TFSA. Buying and selling inside the account is not a withdrawal. Moving sale proceeds out to a bank account and back again is. CRA says an amount withdrawn is added back to contribution room only on January 1 of the next calendar year, and advises against re-contributing in the same year without room; an over-contribution is taxed at 1% a month while it remains. Keeping the cash pot as a cash or savings holding inside the TFSA avoids that trap.
  • RRSP. CRA says income earned in an RRSP is usually exempt from tax while the funds remain in the plan, and payments from the plan are generally taxed. The pot can also sit inside the plan; taking it out to wait in a bank account would be a taxable withdrawal.
  • Non-registered account. CRA says selling or redeeming mutual fund units can produce a capital gain or loss, with the cost of the units sold based on the average cost of all units held. Dollar-cost averaging never sells; strict value averaging does, so it can realize taxable gains in good years. Interest earned on a pot held in cash is generally taxable each year, as the after-tax interest guide shows. Setting the calculator to never sell avoids the sales but leaves more cash waiting after rallies.

A fund is not tax-exempt in itself: the same fund units are taxed differently depending on the account they sit in.

06

Practical choices

  • This is a rule for earnings, not for a lump sum. Value averaging, like dollar-cost averaging, is usually applied to money saved from pay as it arrives. If you already have a large sum and are deciding how fast to invest it, that is a different question, about staging money that could be invested today; the phased-investing guide covers it.
  • Decide where the crash money comes from before the crash. The starting cash and the pot are the only sources in the calculator. With no starting cash the pot runs short in 19 months in the default crash; with CAD 10,000 it never does. Emergency savings should not double as the buying fund, as the income-interruption guide explains.
  • A crash is when the rule is hardest to follow. Value averaging asks for the largest purchases when the news is worst and, often, when jobs are least secure. A rule you abandon halfway through the fall is worse than a simpler one you keep. The guide to pausing contributions in a crash shows what stopping costs.
  • Judge the result by total money, not average price. A lower average cost per unit can coexist with less money overall, because the comparison leaves out the cash that never got invested. The return-measure guide explains why timing contributions changes the money-weighted return but not the fund’s own return.
  • New contributions can rebalance without sales. In a balanced portfolio, sending new money to the part that has fallen is another way to buy what is cheap without selling in a taxable account; see rebalancing with new contributions.

07

What the calculator leaves out

  • One crash, spread evenly through a single year, with smooth returns otherwise. Real markets can fall further, fall more than once, fall within weeks or take many years to recover; a recovery by any particular date is not assured.
  • The fund return is after fees. Fees are charged every year whatever rule you use; frequent trading can add costs, and some funds charge short-term trading fees.
  • No tax is calculated, savings do not rise with pay or prices, and the target is not reset after a missed month. Many investors cap the purchase or raise the target with inflation, which changes the results.
  • The calculator ignores what else the cash in the pot could have done, such as paying down debt.
  • None of this predicts the returns of any fund. Both rules leave you fully exposed to the market once the money is invested.
